title: DSA Practice
description: A short interview sprint through common array, string, stack, linked-list, search, and tree patterns.
sourcePolicy: Problem identities link to LeetCode. Explanations and solutions are original learning content. Difficulty labels can change on the source site.

methodReference.title: Chai Visual DSA
methodReference.usedFor: Compare the obvious approach with a better approach and explain why the complexity changes.

concepts.title: Loops and nested loops
concepts.summary: A loop repeats work over data. One full pass is usually O(n). A loop inside another full loop is usually O(n²).
howItWorks: Use a single loop when each item needs one visit.
Use nested loops for combinations such as every pair.
Look for repeated inner work that a Set or Map can replace.
concepts.complexity: One pass: O(n). Two full nested passes: O(n²).
pitfalls: Do not assume every nested loop is O(n²); pointer movement may still total O(n).
Check loop boundaries and empty input.

concepts.title: Hash Map
concepts.summary: A Map stores key-value pairs. It is useful when you need fast lookup, counts, indices, or cached results.
howItWorks: Choose a value that can act as the key.
Store the information you will need later.
Check the Map instead of scanning old items again.
concepts.complexity: Average get, set, and has: O(1). Up to O(n) stored keys.
pitfalls: Objects are valid Map keys by identity.
A Map uses more memory to remove repeated scans.

concepts.title: Set
concepts.summary: A Set stores unique values. It answers whether a value has appeared before.
howItWorks: Check has(value).
If absent, add(value).
A second occurrence is detected without scanning earlier items.
concepts.complexity: Average has and add: O(1). Up to O(n) stored values.
pitfalls: A Set does not store counts.
Two separate object values are different unless they are the same reference.

concepts.title: Frequency Map
concepts.summary: A frequency map stores how many times each value appears.
howItWorks: Read the old count or zero.
Add one while collecting values.
Subtract or compare counts when matching another input.
concepts.complexity: O(n) time and O(k) space for k distinct values.
pitfalls: Presence alone is not enough when duplicates matter.
Remove or check zero counts carefully.

concepts.title: Stack
concepts.summary: A stack is last-in-first-out. The most recently added item is removed first.
howItWorks: Push when opening work begins.
Read or pop the most recent unfinished item.
Use it for nested brackets, undo, and iterative depth-first search.
concepts.complexity: Push and pop are O(1). Space is O(n) in the worst case.
pitfalls: Check for an empty stack before using the top.
A queue has different first-in-first-out behavior.

concepts.title: Running minimum or maximum
concepts.summary: Keep the best value seen so far while scanning once.
howItWorks: Start with a safe initial value.
Update the running minimum or maximum at each item.
Use it to calculate the best answer ending at the current position.
concepts.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
concepts.example:
let minimum = Infinity;
for (const value of nums) minimum = Math.min(minimum, value);
pitfalls: Respect ordering rules such as buy before sell.
Choose an initial value that works for negative input.

concepts.title: Binary Search
concepts.summary: Binary search repeatedly discards half of a sorted search range.
howItWorks: Keep inclusive left and right boundaries.
Compare the middle value with the target.
Move past the middle into the only possible half.
concepts.complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) space for the iterative form.
pitfalls: The input or search condition must have an ordered property.
Always move beyond mid or the loop may never end.

concepts.title: Two Pointers
concepts.summary: Two pointers track two positions and move according to a rule instead of restarting a scan.
howItWorks: Pointers may start at opposite ends or move at different speeds.
Use a comparison to decide which pointer moves.
Prove that the discarded position cannot be part of a better answer.
concepts.complexity: Often O(n) time because each pointer moves only across the input once.
pitfalls: Two pointers often need sorted data.
Do not move both pointers unless the rule proves it is safe.

concepts.title: In-place array writing
concepts.summary: A read pointer scans values while a write pointer marks the next correct output position.
howItWorks: Read every input value.
Write only values that should stay.
Fill or ignore the remaining tail as required.
concepts.complexity: Usually O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
pitfalls: Do not overwrite unread values.
Preserve order when the prompt requires stable output.

concepts.title: Kadane’s Algorithm
concepts.summary: Kadane’s algorithm finds the best non-empty continuous sum ending at each position.
howItWorks: At each item, choose between starting fresh and extending the old sum.
Store the best sum ending here.
Also store the best sum found anywhere.
concepts.example:
current = Math.max(value, current + value);
best = Math.max(best, current);
pitfalls: An empty subarray is not allowed in Maximum Subarray.
Initialize from the first item to handle all-negative arrays.

concepts.title: Sliding Window
concepts.summary: A sliding window keeps a useful continuous range and moves its boundaries instead of restarting.
howItWorks: Move right to include new data.
Move left until the window becomes valid again.
Measure or update the answer from the valid window.
concepts.complexity: Often O(n) time when each boundary only moves forward.
pitfalls: Use it for continuous ranges, not arbitrary subsequences.
Do not move left backward after it advances.

concepts.title: Prefix and suffix values
concepts.summary: Prefix data summarizes everything before a position; suffix data summarizes everything after it.
howItWorks: Build left-side results in a forward pass.
Carry a right-side value in a backward pass.
Combine both sides for each position.
concepts.complexity: Usually O(n) time. Extra space can be O(1) when the output array stores one side.
pitfalls: Define whether the current item is included.
Zeros need care when using products.

concepts.title: Sorting
concepts.summary: Sorting creates order that makes duplicates, intervals, and pointer decisions easier to manage.
howItWorks: Sort with the correct comparator.
Scan related values next to each other.
Use the order to stop early or move pointers.
concepts.complexity: Comparison sorting is usually O(n log n). JavaScript numeric sort needs (a, b) => a - b.
pitfalls: Default JavaScript sort compares strings.
Sorting may change the input and original indices.

concepts.title: Interval sweep
concepts.summary: After sorting intervals by start, compare each interval with the last merged result.
howItWorks: Sort by start.
Merge when the next start is at or before the last end.
Otherwise start a new result interval.
concepts.complexity: O(n log n) time for sorting and O(n) result space.
concepts.example:
if (start <= last[1]) last[1] = Math.max(last[1], end);
else result.push([start, end]);
pitfalls: Touching endpoints may count as overlap.
Copy interval arrays if mutating input is undesirable.

concepts.title: Linked-list pointers
concepts.summary: Linked-list algorithms change or compare node references instead of array indices.
howItWorks: Save next before changing a link.
Use a dummy head when the real head may change.
Advance only the pointer whose node you consumed.
concepts.complexity: A full traversal is O(n). Many pointer changes use O(1) space.
pitfalls: Losing the remaining list after changing next.
Comparing node values when identity matters.

concepts.title: Fast and slow pointers
concepts.summary: Two linked-list pointers moving at different speeds can find a middle or detect a cycle.
howItWorks: Move slow one step.
Move fast two steps.
Use fast reaching null for a middle, or pointer equality for a cycle.
pitfalls: Check fast and fast.next before moving twice.
Compare node references for cycle detection.

concepts.title: Recursion and depth-first search
concepts.summary: DFS follows one branch deeply before returning. Recursion stores unfinished calls on the call stack.
howItWorks: Write a base case.
Solve smaller child problems.
Combine their returned values for the current node.
concepts.complexity: Tree traversal is O(n) time. Call-stack space is O(h) for tree height h.
pitfalls: Missing a base case causes infinite recursion.
A very deep tree can exceed the call-stack limit.

concepts.title: Queue and breadth-first search
concepts.summary: BFS processes nodes in first-in-first-out order, usually one level or distance at a time.
howItWorks: Add the start node to a queue.
Process the current level boundary.
Append children or neighbors for later processing.
concepts.complexity: O(n) traversal time and O(w) queue space for maximum width w.
pitfalls: Do not use a growing queue length as the current level boundary.
Repeated Array.shift() can add reindexing cost in JavaScript.

intro.title: Intro: solve before you code
intro.purpose: Learn only the terms and habits needed for this two-hour practice set.
learningLoop: Read the prompt and restate the input, output, and rules.
Try a small example by hand.
Name the obvious solution first. It gives you a correct starting point.
Look for repeated work. A set, map, stack, pointer, window, or queue often removes it.
Say the time and space cost before coding.
Code from memory, test an edge case, and explain why it works.

terms.name: Data structure
terms.meaning: A way to organize data. Arrays keep order. Sets keep unique values. Maps connect keys to values. Stacks use last-in-first-out. Queues use first-in-first-out.

terms.name: Algorithm
terms.meaning: A clear sequence of steps that turns an input into the required output.

terms.name: n
terms.meaning: The input size. For an array, n normally means its length.

terms.name: Time complexity
terms.meaning: How the amount of work grows as n grows. O(1) stays constant, O(log n) cuts the work repeatedly, O(n) scans once, O(n log n) often sorts, and O(n²) often checks every pair.

terms.name: Space complexity
terms.meaning: How much extra memory the solution needs. Do not count the returned answer unless the problem asks you to.

terms.name: Brute force
terms.meaning: The direct correct method. It may repeat work, but it helps you understand the problem and gives you a fallback.

terms.name: Optimized method
terms.meaning: A correct method that removes repeated work or uses a useful property such as sorted order.

terms.name: In place
terms.meaning: Change the given structure while using only a small fixed amount of extra memory.

terms.name: Edge case
terms.meaning: A small or unusual valid input, such as an empty list, one item, duplicates, negative values, or a missing target.

terms.name: Invariant
terms.meaning: A fact that stays true while the algorithm runs. Example: everything before a write pointer is already in the correct position.

terms.name: Recursion and call stack
terms.meaning: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem. Each unfinished call uses stack space until it returns.

patternSignals.signal: Find a value or count quickly

interviewScript: Clarify the input and return value.
State a correct simple method and its cost.
Explain the repeated work or useful property.
Propose the better method and its cost.
Dry-run one example before writing code.
sprintPlan: When time ends, mark the problem for another pass. Do not turn this sprint into memorizing code.

problems.title: Two Sum
problems.prompt: Return the indices of two different numbers whose sum equals the target. Assume one answer exists.
beforeCoding: A pair needs nums[i] + nums[j] = target.
For the current value x, the missing value is target - x.
Store values you have already seen with their indices.

basic.name: Check every pair
basic.idea: Try each number with every later number.
steps: Use an outer index i.
Use an inner index j starting at i + 1.
Return when the pair reaches target.

advanced.name: Remember the needed partner
advanced.idea: A map changes the partner lookup from a scan into a constant-time check.
steps: Create a map from value to index.
For each value, check whether its partner is already in the map.
Check first, then store, so one element is never reused.

dryRun: At 2, need 7. Store 2 → 0.
At 7, need 2. The map has it, so return [0, 1].
mistakes: Storing before checking can reuse the current item.
Returning values instead of indices.
finishCheck: Explain the main idea without reading the solution.
Write the better solution again from a blank editor.
Test one normal case and one edge case.

problems.title: Contains Duplicate
problems.prompt: Return true when any value appears at least twice. Otherwise return false.
beforeCoding: The exact positions do not matter.
You only need to know whether a value was seen before.
A Set stores unique values.

basic.name: Compare every pair
basic.idea: If any two positions contain the same value, a duplicate exists.
steps: Check each i against every later j.
Return true on equality.
Return false after all pairs.

advanced.name: Track seen values
advanced.idea: A Set answers “have I seen this?” without another scan.
steps: Create an empty Set.
For each value, return true if it is already present.
Otherwise add it and continue.

dryRun: See 1, 2, and 3 for the first time.
See 1 again; it is already in the Set.
mistakes: Comparing a Set size after changing the input unnecessarily.
Forgetting that Set lookup is the reason the method is faster.
finishCheck: Explain the main idea without reading the solution.
Write the better solution again from a blank editor.
Test one normal case and one edge case.

problems.title: Valid Anagram
problems.prompt: Return true when two strings contain the same characters with the same counts in a different or identical order.
beforeCoding: Different lengths can never be anagrams.
Order does not matter, but frequency does.
You can sort both strings or count characters.

basic.name: Sort both strings
basic.idea: Equal sorted forms contain the same characters with the same counts.
steps: Reject different lengths.
Split, sort, and join each string.
Compare the results.

advanced.name: Count characters
advanced.idea: One pass adds counts from the first string; another pass removes them with the second.
steps: Reject different lengths.
Build a Map of counts from s.
Decrease for t; fail if a needed count is missing.

dryRun: Count anagram: a3, n1, g1, r1, m1.
Removing nagaram reaches zero for every character.
mistakes: Checking only whether characters exist, not how often.
Forgetting the quick length check.
finishCheck: Explain the main idea without reading the solution.
Write the better solution again from a blank editor.
Test one normal case and one edge case.

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.prompt: Check whether every opening bracket is closed by the same type in the correct order.
beforeCoding: The most recent unmatched opening bracket must close first.
That is last-in-first-out behavior.
A stack represents unmatched opening brackets.

basic.name: Remove valid pairs repeatedly
basic.idea: Delete (), [], and {} until no more changes are possible.
steps: Keep the previous string.
Replace all valid pairs with empty text.
The input is valid only if nothing remains.

advanced.name: Use a stack
advanced.idea: Push opening brackets. A closing bracket must match the top item.
steps: Map each closing bracket to its opening partner.
Push opening brackets.
On a closing bracket, pop and compare.

dryRun: Push ( then [.
The next ) expects (, but the top is [. Return false.
mistakes: Matching a closing bracket with any earlier opener instead of the latest one.
Forgetting to reject leftover opening brackets.
finishCheck: Explain the main idea without reading the solution.
Write the better solution again from a blank editor.
Test one normal case and one edge case.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
problems.prompt: Choose one day to buy and a later day to sell. Return the largest profit, or zero if no profit is possible.
beforeCoding: The sell day must come after the buy day.
For each sell price, you need the smallest earlier price.
Keep that minimum while scanning once.

basic.name: Try every buy and sell day
basic.idea: Calculate every valid later selling profit.
steps: Choose each buy index.
Try each later sell index.
Keep the largest positive difference.

advanced.name: Track the lowest earlier price
advanced.idea: The best sale today uses the lowest price seen before or today.
steps: Start minimum at Infinity and best profit at zero.
Update the minimum with each price.
Compare best with price minus minimum.

dryRun: Minimum becomes 1 on day two.
At price 6, profit is 6 - 1 = 5.
mistakes: Allowing a sale before the buy.
Returning a negative profit instead of zero.
finishCheck: Explain the main idea without reading the solution.
Write the better solution again from a blank editor.
Test one normal case and one edge case.

problems.title: Binary Search
problems.prompt: Find a target in an ascending sorted array. Return its index, or -1 when it is absent.
beforeCoding: The sorted order tells you which half cannot contain the target.
The search range is inclusive from left to right.
Discard half after every comparison.

basic.name: Linear scan
basic.idea: Visit values from left to right until the target appears.
steps: Loop through every index.
Return an index on equality.
Return -1 after the loop.

advanced.name: Binary search
advanced.idea: Compare the middle value and keep only the possible half.
steps: Set left to 0 and right to length - 1.
Calculate the middle safely.
Move left or right past middle.

dryRun: Middle value 3 is too small, so discard the left half.
Middle value 9 matches at index 4.
mistakes: Using binary search on unsorted input.
Writing left < right and missing a one-item range.
finishCheck: Explain the main idea without reading the solution.
Write the better solution again from a blank editor.
Test one normal case and one edge case.

problems.title: Move Zeroes
problems.prompt: Move all zero values to the end in place while preserving the order of non-zero values.
beforeCoding: One pointer reads every value.
Another pointer marks where the next non-zero value belongs.
After writing non-zero values, fill the rest with zeroes.

basic.name: Build a separate array
basic.idea: Collect non-zero values, append zeroes, then copy back.
steps: Filter or collect every non-zero value.
Append enough zeroes.
Copy the result into the input array.

advanced.name: Write in place
advanced.idea: Compact non-zero values at the front and overwrite the unused tail with zeroes.
steps: Set write to zero.
Write each non-zero value and advance write.
Fill from write to the end with zero.

dryRun: Read 1 and write it at index 0.
Then write 3 and 12. Fill the last two positions with zero.
mistakes: Changing the relative order of non-zero values.
Returning a new array when the problem asks for in-place changes.
finishCheck: Explain the main idea without reading the solution.
Write the better solution again from a blank editor.
Test one normal case and one edge case.

problems.title: Merge Sorted Array
problems.prompt: Merge the first m values of nums1 with n values of nums2 into nums1, which already has enough empty space.
beforeCoding: Both useful parts are already sorted.
Writing from the front may destroy unread nums1 values.
The largest remaining value belongs at the last open position.

basic.name: Combine and sort
basic.idea: Create the combined useful values, sort them, and copy back.
steps: Take nums1 up to m.
Add nums2 up to n and sort numerically.
Copy all values into nums1.

advanced.name: Fill from the end
advanced.idea: Compare the largest unread values and place the larger one in the final open slot.
steps: Set pointers at m - 1, n - 1, and m + n - 1.
Write the larger value and move its pointer.
Copy remaining nums2 values.

dryRun: Compare 3 and 6; write 6 at the end.
Compare 3 and 5; write 5. Continue until nums2 is empty.
mistakes: Sorting numbers without a numeric comparator in JavaScript.
Writing from the front and overwriting unread values.
finishCheck: Explain the main idea without reading the solution.
Write the better solution again from a blank editor.
Test one normal case and one edge case.

problems.title: Maximum Subarray
problems.prompt: Return the largest sum of a non-empty continuous section of the array.
beforeCoding: A subarray must be continuous.
At each value, either start a new subarray or extend the previous one.
Keep the best sum ending here and the best sum overall.

basic.name: Try every starting point
basic.idea: Add every possible continuous section and keep the largest sum.
steps: Choose a start index.
Extend an end index while updating a running sum.
Keep the largest seen sum.

advanced.name: Kadane’s algorithm
advanced.idea: A negative previous total cannot help a future subarray, so start fresh when the current value is better.
steps: Set current and best to the first value.
For each later value, choose value alone or current + value.
Update the global best.

dryRun: At 4, starting fresh beats extending the negative sum.
Extend through -1, 2, and 1 to reach 6.
mistakes: Allowing an empty subarray and returning zero for all-negative input.
Confusing a subarray with a subsequence.
finishCheck: Explain the main idea without reading the solution.
Write the better solution again from a blank editor.
Test one normal case and one edge case.

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.prompt: Return the length of the longest continuous string section that contains no repeated character.
beforeCoding: The answer is a continuous window.
Expand right while characters stay unique.
When a duplicate appears, move left beyond its previous position.

basic.name: Start at every position
basic.idea: Grow a unique-character Set from every possible start.
steps: Choose a start index.
Extend right until a duplicate appears.
Record the largest Set size.

advanced.name: Sliding window with last positions
advanced.idea: Each character enters once, and left jumps past a duplicate instead of restarting.
steps: Map characters to their latest indices.
Move left to max(left, old index + 1).
Update the best window length.

dryRun: Window abc has length 3.
The next a moves left from 0 to 1, giving bca.
mistakes: Moving left backward when an old duplicate is outside the window.
Treating substring as non-continuous.
finishCheck: Explain the main idea without reading the solution.
Write the better solution again from a blank editor.
Test one normal case and one edge case.

problems.title: Product of Array Except Self
problems.prompt: Build an answer where each position contains the product of all other input values, without division.
beforeCoding: For index i, split the product into values before i and values after i.
A left pass can store prefix products in the answer.
A right pass can multiply a running suffix without another array.

basic.name: Multiply all other positions
basic.idea: For each output index, scan the entire input and skip that index.
steps: Create an answer array.
For each i, start product at 1.
Multiply nums[j] when j is not i.

advanced.name: Prefix then suffix products
advanced.idea: Reuse products accumulated from each side.
steps: Store the product before each index in answer.
Walk right to left with a suffix product.
Multiply answer by suffix, then update suffix.

dryRun: Prefix answer becomes [1,1,2,6].
Right pass multiplies suffixes 1,4,12,24.
mistakes: Using division, which breaks the stated rule and needs special zero handling.
Counting the returned array as extra working space when the problem excludes it.
finishCheck: Explain the main idea without reading the solution.
Write the better solution again from a blank editor.
Test one normal case and one edge case.

problems.title: 3Sum
problems.prompt: Return every unique triplet of values whose sum is zero. Do not return duplicate triplets.
beforeCoding: Sorting puts equal values together and lets pointers react to the sum.
Fix one value, then solve a two-sum problem to its right.
Skip equal fixed and pointer values to avoid duplicate answers.

basic.name: Try every triplet
basic.idea: Check every i, j, k combination and use a Set to remove duplicate value groups.
steps: Use three increasing indices.
When the sum is zero, sort the triplet key.
Store only unseen keys.

advanced.name: Sort and use two pointers
advanced.idea: After fixing nums[i], increasing left raises the sum and decreasing right lowers it.
steps: Sort numerically.
Skip a repeated fixed value.
Move left and right, recording zero sums and skipping duplicates.

dryRun: Sorted input starts -4,-1,-1,0,1,2.
Fix -1. Pointers find -1 + -1 + 2 and -1 + 0 + 1.
mistakes: Forgetting numeric sort in JavaScript.
Returning duplicate triplets.
finishCheck: Explain the main idea without reading the solution.
Write the better solution again from a blank editor.
Test one normal case and one edge case.

problems.title: Merge Intervals
problems.prompt: Combine every overlapping interval and return the non-overlapping result.
beforeCoding: After sorting by start, only the last merged interval can overlap the next one.
Overlap exists when next start is not greater than the last end.
Extend the end to the larger end.

basic.name: Repeatedly search for overlaps
basic.idea: Merge one overlapping pair, remove it, and restart until nothing changes.
steps: Copy the intervals.
Find any overlapping pair.
Replace it with their combined interval and repeat.

advanced.name: Sort and sweep once
advanced.idea: Sorted starts make each new interval comparable with only the latest merged interval.
steps: Sort by start.
Start result with the first interval.
Merge overlap into the last result or append a new interval.

dryRun: [1,3] and [2,6] overlap, so the last result becomes [1,6].
[8,10] starts after 6, so append it.
mistakes: Skipping the initial sort.
Using start < end and missing intervals that touch at one point.
finishCheck: Explain the main idea without reading the solution.
Write the better solution again from a blank editor.
Test one normal case and one edge case.

problems.title: Reverse Linked List
problems.prompt: Reverse a singly linked list and return its new head.
beforeCoding: Changing next loses the rest of the list unless you save it first.
Keep previous, current, and next references.
After the loop, previous is the new head.

basic.name: Store nodes first
basic.idea: Put nodes in an array, then connect them in reverse order.
steps: Walk the list and push every node.
Link each later node to the previous array item.
Set the old head next to null.

advanced.name: Reverse pointers in place
advanced.idea: Save the next node, point current backward, then advance both pointers.
steps: Set previous to null and current to head.
Save current.next.
Reverse current.next, then move previous and current.

dryRun: At node 1, save 2 and point 1 to null.
At node 2, save 3 and point 2 to 1.
mistakes: Changing current.next before saving it.
Returning current, which is null after the loop.
finishCheck: Explain the main idea without reading the solution.
Write the better solution again from a blank editor.
Test one normal case and one edge case.

problems.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
problems.prompt: Merge two ascending linked lists into one ascending list and return its head.
beforeCoding: The smaller head must be the next output node.
A dummy node removes the special case for the first node.
When one list ends, append the rest of the other.

basic.name: Collect values and rebuild
basic.idea: Read all values, sort them, and build a new list.
steps: Collect values from both lists.
Sort numerically.
Create new nodes in sorted order.

advanced.name: Splice with two pointers
advanced.idea: Always attach the smaller current node, then advance only that list.
steps: Create dummy and tail.
Compare list1.val and list2.val while both exist.
Attach the remaining list.

dryRun: Compare 1 and 1; attach the first list node.
Compare 2 and 1; attach the second list node.
mistakes: Forgetting to move tail.
Losing the rest of a list after the main loop.
finishCheck: Explain the main idea without reading the solution.
Write the better solution again from a blank editor.
Test one normal case and one edge case.

problems.title: Middle of the Linked List
problems.prompt: Return the middle node. With two middle nodes, return the second one.
beforeCoding: A fast pointer moves twice for each slow step.
When fast reaches the end, slow has covered half the distance.
The loop condition controls the second-middle rule.

basic.name: Store every node
basic.idea: An array gives direct access to the floor(length / 2) node.
steps: Walk the list and collect node references.
Calculate floor(length / 2).
Return that node.

advanced.name: Fast and slow pointers
advanced.idea: Fast covers two links while slow covers one, so slow stops in the middle.
steps: Start both at head.
While fast and fast.next exist, advance slow once and fast twice.
Return slow.

dryRun: With six nodes, slow visits 1,2,3,4 while fast visits 1,3,5,end.
Slow finishes at the second middle, node 4.
mistakes: Using fast.next.next without checking fast and fast.next.
Returning the first middle when the prompt requires the second.
finishCheck: Explain the main idea without reading the solution.
Write the better solution again from a blank editor.
Test one normal case and one edge case.

problems.title: Linked List Cycle
problems.prompt: Return true when following next pointers eventually visits a node again.
examples: 3→2→0→-4 with the last node pointing to node 2 → true
beforeCoding: A cycle repeats a node reference, not merely a value.
A Set can remember references.
Inside a cycle, a pointer moving twice as fast eventually meets the slow pointer.

basic.name: Remember visited nodes
basic.idea: If a node reference is already in the Set, the list has looped.
steps: Create a Set.
Check and add each node while moving forward.
Return false if null is reached.

advanced.name: Floyd’s cycle detection
advanced.idea: If there is a loop, fast cannot escape and must catch slow.
steps: Start both pointers at head.
Move slow once and fast twice.
Return true if they meet; false if fast reaches null.

dryRun: Fast enters the cycle ahead of slow.
Their distance shrinks around the loop until both references match.
mistakes: Comparing node values instead of node references.
Dereferencing fast.next without checking it.
finishCheck: Explain the main idea without reading the solution.
Write the better solution again from a blank editor.

problems.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
problems.prompt: Return the number of nodes on the longest path from the root to a leaf. An empty tree has depth zero.
beforeCoding: A tree answer often depends on answers from left and right subtrees.
Depth is one for the current node plus the larger child depth.
The empty base case returns zero.

basic.name: Recursive depth-first search
basic.idea: Ask each child for its depth and keep the larger result.
steps: Return zero for null.
Find left and right depth recursively.
Return one plus their maximum.

advanced.name: Iterative breadth-first search
advanced.idea: Process one complete tree level at a time and count levels.
steps: Return zero for null.
Put root in a queue.
For each level, remove exactly its current node count and add children.

dryRun: Root is level 1.
Nodes 9 and 20 form level 2; nodes 15 and 7 form level 3.
mistakes: Counting edges when the prompt counts nodes.
Missing the null-root base case.

problems.title: Invert Binary Tree
problems.prompt: Mirror a binary tree by swapping the left and right child of every node.
examples: Root 4 with children 2 and 7 becomes root 4 with children 7 and 2
beforeCoding: Every node needs the same local operation: swap its children.
Then repeat on both resulting subtrees.
A recursive or queue traversal can visit every node once.

basic.name: Recursive depth-first search
basic.idea: Swap at the current node, then invert both children.
steps: Return null for an empty node.
Swap left and right.
Recursively invert both children.

advanced.name: Iterative breadth-first search
advanced.idea: A queue avoids recursive call-stack growth on a very deep tree.
steps: Return null for empty root.
Queue the root.
Remove a node, swap its children, and queue non-null children.

dryRun: Swap the root children first.
Then swap the children of each node on the next level.
mistakes: Only swapping the root.
Queuing null children and trying to access their fields.

problems.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
problems.prompt: Return the tree values grouped from top to bottom, one array for each depth level.
beforeCoding: A queue keeps nodes in first-in-first-out order.
The queue length at the start of a level tells you how many nodes belong to that level.
Add children for the next level after reading each node.

basic.name: Depth-first search with a depth value
basic.idea: Use the recursion depth as the result-array index.
steps: Create an empty result.
When a depth is first seen, create its array.
Push the value, then visit children with depth + 1.

advanced.name: Queue one level at a time
advanced.idea: Capture the queue boundary before adding the next level’s children.
steps: Return [] for null root.
Queue the root.
For each level size, remove that many nodes and collect their values.

dryRun: Queue starts with [3], so first level is [3].
Its children create the next boundary [9,20], followed by [15,7].
mistakes: Using the growing queue length inside the same level loop.
Calling shift repeatedly in JavaScript and adding avoidable array reindexing cost.
